paper_metadata.title: Longitudinal white matter microstructural changes in pediatric mild traumatic brain injury: An A-CAP study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a large, multi-center prospective cohort design with clearly defined inclusion/exclusion criteria and a well-matched orthopedic injury (OI) control group. The source population and recruitment methods are thoroughly described.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: A-CAP recruited children between 8–16.99 years of age who presented within 48 h of sustaining an mTBI or OI to the emergency department (ED) of five children's hospitals across Canada
items.reasoning: The target population is clearly defined by age, injury type, and clinical setting (ED).

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: This multisite study used a prospective, concurrent cohort design... recruited from five pediatric emergency departments.
items.reasoning: Recruitment from multiple EDs across Canada provides a robust sampling frame for pediatric trauma.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While the study protocol is cited (Yeates et al., 2017), the specific calendar dates for the recruitment period are not explicitly stated in this manuscript.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Alberta Children's Hospital (Calgary), Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (Ottawa), Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sainte-Justine (Montreal), Stollery Children's Hospital (Edmonton), and British Columbia Children's Hospital (Vancouver)
items.reasoning: Specific hospitals and cities are listed.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: consistent with the World Health Organization (WHO) definition of mTBI: (i) observed loss of consciousness, (ii) glasgow coma scale score of 13–14, or (iii) at least one acute sign or symptom of concussion
items.reasoning: Detailed clinical criteria for both mTBI and OI groups are provided, including AIS scores and specific exclusion thresholds.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Of 3075 eligible children with mTBI or mild OI, 967 consented to participate in A-CAP
items.reasoning: The participation rate is approximately 31% (967/3075). While low, this is common in imaging studies; however, it introduces potential selection bias compared to the >80% ideal.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1: Age, Sex, Parental education, Race, Mechanism of injury, Sport-related injury, Symptom ratings.
items.reasoning: Comprehensive demographic and clinical baseline data are provided in Table 1.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Attrition rates are transparently reported and comparable between groups. The authors analyzed differences between completers and non-completers, finding only minor differences in parental education at the 6-month mark.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: A total of 407 children (73%) had usable longitudinal DTI data at post-acute and 3 months... or 6 months assessments.
items.reasoning: A 73% retention rate for longitudinal neuroimaging is considered high and adequate.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text describes the rates of attrition but does not detail specific efforts to re-engage or collect data from dropouts.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: New MRI contraindications (after recruitment, e.g., orthodontia treatment) and scheduling difficulties were the most common reasons that MRI was not completed.
items.reasoning: Specific reasons for missing imaging data are provided in the Figure 1 caption.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Children who returned at post-acute, 3 months, and/or 6 months did not differ from those who did not return in terms of age, sex, race, or parental education, with one exception: Children who returned at 6 months had higher parental education
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly compared completers and non-completers on key demographic variables.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Children who returned... did not differ from those who did not return in terms of age, sex, race, or parental education
items.reasoning: Statistical comparison confirmed minimal differences, suggesting attrition was largely non-informative.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (mTBI vs OI and symptom status) is well-defined. DTI measurement used standardized protocols across sites and included a rigorous quality assurance process and harmonization (ComBAT) to account for scanner differences.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Children in the mTBI group sustained a blunt head trauma resulting in at least one of the following three criteria... consistent with the World Health Organization (WHO) definition
items.reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (injury group) and the secondary factor (symptom status) are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The Health and Behavior Inventory was used to assess cognitive and somatic symptoms. This measure has good internal consistency and test–retest reliability
items.reasoning: The symptom status classification used a validated tool and a Reliable Change Index (RCI) to minimize measurement error.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Results were used to classify children with mTBI into two groups using a critical z-score >1.65 (one-tailed p <.05)
items.reasoning: The cut-point for persistent symptoms was based on a standard statistical threshold (z > 1.65) rather than data-driven optimization.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Thirty diffusion-weighted images... were acquired at b = 900 s/mm2... with 2.2 mm isotropic resolution at all sites
items.reasoning: Standardized MRI protocols were used across all five sites.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Persistent symptom status based on child and parent report was available for 275 (76%) and 286 (79%) children with mTBI
items.reasoning: While high, approximately 20-25% of the mTBI group lacked symptom status data for the sub-analysis.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study does not mention imputation for missing symptom data; it appears to use available-case analysis.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcomes (DTI metrics) are objective biological measures. The use of automated tractography (AFQ) and ComBAT harmonization reduces subjective bias and site-related measurement error.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Mean diffusivity (MD) and fractional anisotropy (FA) were derived for 18 white matter tracts
items.reasoning: The DTI metrics and the specific tracts of interest are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Automated deterministic tractography was performed using the open-source Automated Fiber Quantification software package v1.2
items.reasoning: Automated methods reduce manual tracing bias, and visual quality checks were performed by trained analysts.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Thirty diffusion-weighted images... were acquired... with 2.2 mm isotropic resolution at all sites
items.reasoning: The imaging protocol was standardized across the multi-site study.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study rigorously accounts for confounding through both design (OI control group) and analysis (LME models adjusting for age, sex, and site).

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: investigate the relations of group (mTBI, OI), the linear and quadratic effects of time (days) post-injury, age at injury, sex
items.reasoning: Key demographic and temporal confounders were measured and included in the models.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: age at injury, sex, race, parental education, days post-injury
items.reasoning: Confounders are standard demographic and clinical variables.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Information about acute clinical presentation was collected during the initial ED visit, and information on mechanism of injury and a demographic questionnaire was collected
items.reasoning: Data were collected prospectively using standardized forms.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Enrolled participants at each site returned for three additional follow-up assessments
items.reasoning: The follow-up schedule and data collection methods were uniform across sites.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not specify how missing covariate data (e.g., parental education) were handled in the LME models.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Children with OI were chosen for comparison because they are similar to those with mild TBI, both demographically and in terms of risk factors
items.reasoning: The use of an OI control group is a strong design choice to control for the general effects of trauma and demographic factors.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Multiple linear mixed effects models... controlling for the random effect of participant... and fixed generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) predictors
items.reasoning: The statistical models adjusted for age, sex, time, and site (via ComBAT).

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The analysis uses sophisticated mixed-effects modeling appropriate for longitudinal data. Multiple comparison corrections (FDR) were applied, and effect sizes were reported. There is no evidence of selective reporting.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Multiple linear mixed effects models were computed in RStudio using the ImerTest package... The final model was: Harmonized DTI Metric ~ Group * poly(time, 2) * (Age + Sex) + Hemisphere + (1|Participant)
items.reasoning: The exact model formula and software packages are provided.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: investigate the relations of group (mTBI, OI), the linear and quadratic effects of time (days) post-injury, age at injury, sex, and group by time by age, and group by time by sex interactions
items.reasoning: The model includes theoretically relevant interactions (age and sex as moderators).

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: linear mixed effects (LME) modeling... controlling for the random effect of participant
items.reasoning: LME is the gold standard for longitudinal data with missing observations and varying time points.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: False discovery rate (FDR) was used to correct for multiple comparisons... Only the effects with a 95% confidence interval range that excluded 0 were considered to be robust
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings and use FDR to control for Type I error across 18 tracts.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
